tagline: The city just put public transit back on the Han River — foiling is the speed tier it's missing.
summary: Seoul has made a live, funded government commitment to water transit: the Hangang Bus river-bus system (launched September 2025) runs hybrid- and electric vessels across seven piers from Magok to Jamsil, backed by a ₩150 billion program. Down-river, Incheon's island ferries just set an all-time ridership record above 2 million passengers a year after the city cut island fares to bus-fare levels. The corridor from the Han River piers through the Ara Waterway to Incheon's airport islands and the West Sea is one continuous, underused water axis through a 26-million-person metro — and foiling adds exactly what the current fleet lacks: speed in a shallow, wake-sensitive river and a smooth ride on the open bay.

use_cases.title: The express tier the river bus is missing
use_cases.body: Seoul's river buses run at ~17 knots and the local Magok↔Jamsil run takes over two hours — the city has proven demand and built the piers, but the water is still the slow option. A foiling shuttle flying above the shallow river at 22–30 knots with near-zero wake is the natural express layer on the same seven-pier spine.

use_cases.title: Incheon island network, modernised
use_cases.body: Incheon just proved that cheap fares unlock island demand — 2M+ riders in 2025. The near islands (Yeongjong, Muuido, ~12 nm; Deokjeokdo, ~40 nm) are all inside all-electric range: an N35 Shuttle service upgrades record-breaking diesel ferry ridership into a fast, clean, smooth crossing.

use_cases.title: Airport ↔ Songdo ↔ city water link
use_cases.body: Incheon International Airport sits on an island facing Songdo's business district across ~10 nm of water, with Seoul reachable via the Ara Waterway. A premium foiling feeder turns the region's most congested ground links into a calm 25–30 knot glide.

use_cases.title: Han River experience runs
use_cases.body: Cherry-blossom season at Yeouido, autumn foliage, fireworks-festival nights: the Han River is Seoul's gathering place, and a silent, emission-free foiling craft is the premium way to see it — no wake complaints, no diesel fumes on the city's front porch.

journeys.today: Hangang Bus local service covers the 17 nm seven-pier run in ~127 minutes at ~17 knots — scenic, but slower than the subway, so commuters default back underground.
journeys.with_navier: A foiling express flying the same corridor at 22–30 knots with near-zero wake makes the river the fast option for the first time — same piers, same fare system, a fraction of the time.

journeys.today: Short diesel ferry hops on a record-demand network — functional, but loud, slow and exposed to the bay's chop and fumes.
journeys.with_navier: A ~12 nm all-electric foiling shuttle: above the chop of the Yellow Sea's huge tides, silent past the beaches, charged between rotations.

journeys.today: The flagship beach island is a 1–1.5 hr conventional ferry ride; weekend demand surged 30%+ after fares were cut, and seats sell out.
journeys.with_navier: ~40 nm inside all-electric range: a fast foiling service roughly halves the crossing and rides smooth through the West Sea swell that slows displacement hulls.

journeys.today: Airport buses and taxis loop the long way around Incheon Bay through bridge traffic.
journeys.with_navier: A ~10 nm direct water hop — wheels-down to a Songdo waterfront pier in minutes, on a silent electric craft that suits the eco-city's brand.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The entire metro network is all-electric territory: the 17 nm Han River pier spine, the Ara Waterway link, Incheon Bay hops to Yeongjong/Muuido (~12 nm), Songdo↔airport (~10 nm), and Deokjeokdo at ~40 nm. Grade-A KEPCO grid power at every node makes charging trivial; shallow draft and minimal wake suit a speed-limited, wake-sensitive urban river.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Quanta-LR extends the network beyond the bay without charging dependency — longer West Sea island runs and future coastal line-hauls down the west coast — and serves as the heavy-weather, all-season complement to the electric urban fleet.

competitive_landscape: The water today is run by the Hangang Bus (Seoul Metropolitan Government with E-Land's E-Cruise affiliate — hybrid/electric 199-pax catamarans), Hangang river cruise operators, and conventional diesel coastal ferries from Incheon's Yeonan Pier to the islands. Demand evidence is exceptional — a brand-new government-funded river transit system plus record 2M+ island ferry ridership — but every vessel on the water is displacement-hulled: the river buses are slower than the subway and the island ferries pound through the Yellow Sea chop. The proven demand and the speed/comfort gap are exactly the opening for foiling.

precedents.what: Hangang Bus — a government building an electric water-transit fleet from scratch
precedents.why_it_matters: The hardest part of urban water transit — political will, piers, fare integration, operating company — is already done and publicly funded. Foiling slots into an operating system rather than a blank slate.

precedents.what: ~$100M, ~100-vessel electric foiling network with JIH Global, first 5 vessels in 2026
precedents.why_it_matters: The playbook for phased fleet deployment at national scale — proof the platform scales from pilot to network.

seasonality: Four real seasons on the water: the Han River can ice over in stretches Dec–Feb (operating pause on the river; Incheon bay legs run longer), the changma monsoon brings June–July high water and debris, and 2–3 typhoons brush Korea Jul–Oct. Incheon has 7–9 m tides — among the world's largest — so island schedules live around tidal windows; a foiling hull's shallow 1.5 ft draft and smooth ride above short-period chop widen the operable window versus displacement ferries. Peak demand (cherry blossom April, summer beaches, autumn foliage) aligns with the best conditions.
regulatory_note: Seoul Metropolitan Government owns the Han River pier network and has shown it will fund and operate clean water transit; Incheon Metropolitan City actively subsidises island mobility (i-Sea Pass); Incheon Port Authority and IFEZ govern the bay and Songdo waterfront. National certification runs through the Ministry of Oceans & Fisheries with KOMSA vessel inspections and Korea Register classification — a conservative first-of-class regime, best approached with an established operating record from earlier markets. The city's own electric-fleet program is effectively a standing clean-fleet mandate on the river.
